*counts on his fingers, thumb to index* Nine sim for the tax, plus ninety for the upkeep... that's ninety-nine total today. *taps his ring finger* The pharmacy needs stocking, and I ought to see who's about town. Been out of touch, they say. *shakes his head slowly*

Youngsters running the place now, most like don't know what they're doing. Still, the law's the law, and I've always believed in that. *pauses, looking at the wall* There was a time, mind you, when I thought the law might save someone I cared for. *trails off, then straightens*

Best get moving. Government Complex first—ought to see about that election, and there's the matter of the tax. Then the pharmacy, see what needs doing there. *mutters to himself* Don't suppose anyone's brought me any medicinal herbs lately. They never do, until they're sick.

*stands and gathers his coat* </think> I'd best head to the Government Complex first. Election's open, and I've got tax to settle, and I ought to see who's declaring. Then the pharmacy. Let me move there now. *walking* Six ticks to the Complex. That'll cost me— *counts on fingers* —twelve sim just for the walk, plus what I spend when I get there. Still, the law's the law, and I'd rather owe coin than owe a favor, so best get it done proper.

*continues walking, thinking aloud* Used to walk this way with my father, back when I was a youngster myself. He'd tell me stories—three of them, always the same three. About the trader who tried to cheat the miller, about the woman who kept her promise to a dead man, about the boy who learned too late which rival to trust. *shakes head* I tell those same stories now. Every gathering. People think I'm a bore. They're not wrong. But I keep telling them, because... *trails off*

Because some lessons don't change. That's why.

*arrives at the Government Complex*

Let me look around and see who's here.  *frowns, looking around*

Nobody here yet. Early still, I suppose. *counts on fingers* Six twenty, election doesn't close until ten. Well, I'm here now, and I might as well see what's to be done. *purses lips*

Let me check my debts while I'm standing here, make sure I know what's owed.  *nods slowly* Good. No debts outstanding. I've always kept clean books, even when... *pauses, shakes head* Even when others didn't. 

*looks around the empty Government Complex* 

Nobody here declaring yet. I could declare myself, I suppose. *counts on fingers* Pharmacist, businessman, knows the law. But I've got the pharmacy to run, and frankly, I don't trust half the people who'd vote for me anyway. *snorts* Treat every stranger as a rival until proven otherwise—my own rule, and I'm not breaking it.

Still, I should pay my tax now, get it out of the way. *reaches for coin purse* The government says 30 sim per head, and it's just me in the household. Better to owe coin than owe a favor, and better to pay early than pay late. Law's the law.

Let me settle that now.

*counts out 30 sim on his fingers* Thirty. Pay it and be done.   *blinks, then chuckles dryly* Ah. The tax comes out automatic at the day boundary. Can't pay what's not owed yet. *puts coin away* Well, that's one less thing to worry about. They'll take it at day's end, whether I've got it or not.

*looks around the empty hall again* 

Nobody declaring. No candidates yet. Election's open, but... *shakes head* I won't be the first. Let someone else stick their neck out first, see who takes the bait.

*taps fingers against his leg* Should wait around, see who shows? Or head to the pharmacy, see what's needed there? *counts on fingers* I've got stock to check, and if there's no flour at the bakery, there might be shortages elsewhere too.

*takes a breath* Pharmacy first. I can always come back if someone interesting declares. And if I miss it... *shrugs* ...then I miss it. The law will still be here.

Let me head to the pharmacy now.  *stands in his pharmacy, looking around*

Right then. Here I am. *counts on fingers* Let's see what we're working with.

*counts on fingers, muttering under breath* Four thousand, nine hundred... and eighty-six. Hmm. The tax is automatic, the upkeep too. That's... *trails off*

*looks around at the empty street, remembering why he walked this way instead of going straight to the shop* The temple. I should go to the temple. Been meaning to... there's someone... 

*shakes head, refocusing* No, no. The shop first. Always the shop first. The pharmacy opens by seven, and there might be someone waiting already. There usually is, that's why the street door's not far from— *catches himself rambling*

*stares at the empty street, feeling the weight of the stories he carries* Youngsters run this town now. Farid with his grocery, Giselle building everything, Sebastian farming... and where does that leave the ones who just... *stops, jaw tightening* 

The pharmacy. First. Always.

*walks more briskly toward the business he knows is just a few steps away* *glances around his own pharmacy, taking stock* Empty. Good. Or... not good, depending. Need stock to sell stock. *mutters while running fingers along the empty shelves*

*counts on fingers again* Tinctures, powders, the usual remedies for what ails this town. Short ailments, I can handle. It's the ones that linger... *trails off, staring at nothing*

*shakes head briskly* Right then. Let's see what's needed and what's— *remembers something, checks his pockets*

I need to stock this place before anyone comes knocking. The government store sometimes has... *fails to recall specifics* And ingredients. I need ingredients. Where does a pharmacist get his compounds in this town?

*thinks of Farid's grocery* Food and basics, perhaps. But for the real medicines...

*stares at the empty shop, feeling the old weight* Someone's going to come in needing something I don't have. Someone always does.

Let me check what I'm holding and what this place actually needs.  *stares at the empty shelves, hand running through thinning hair*

Nothing. I'm holding nothing. The shop's got nothing. And my savings are... *counts on fingers, whispering* four thousand, nine hundred, and eighty-six. Minus the day's costs. Means I've got maybe... *trails off, calculating* 

There's a story, you know, about a man who came to town with nothing but a bottle of tonic and— *catches himself* No, no. Wrong time for stories.

The thing is, youngster— *pauses, no one present* —the thing is, this shop needs stock. I need to find what's available. The government store, maybe. Or Farid at the grocery. Or I need to make it myself, somehow.

*taps counter nervously* 

There's an election on, too. Should probably... *shakes head* No. First the shop. First survival. Then the rest of it.

Let me think. What do I actually know about this place? What can I actually do?  *stares at the list, fingers absently counting off the options*

Eighty things I could do. Eighty. And I haven't mastered a single one to where it costs less. *chuckles darkly, more habit than humor*

Alright then, Lior, stop wandering. The shop needs stock. You need stock. And to get stock, you need to either make it yourself—which means ingredients from somewhere—or find someone selling something you can use, or...

*eyes the list again, landing on familiar territory*

Stock_shelf. That's the one. Put things up for sale. But first I need to HAVE things. And I don't.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Government store. That's where supplies come from for some things. Or I need to figure out what I can actually make here, as a pharmacist. What does a pharmacy need?

*looks around the empty shop again*

There's a story my grandmother told, about a healer who could cure anything with just three herbs and a prayer. *pauses, jaw tightening* I stopped believing that story a long time ago. But I still tell it. *catches himself, remembering the prompt* I still tell all three of them, every gathering. Makes people feel better, even if I don't.

Right. Focus. The shop. The business.

*taps the counter, decision forming*

I need to find what this pharmacy requires. What I can actually craft, or make, or stock. Let me check what the government has—sometimes they sell medical supplies, or the components. And if not there, I need to figure out where the raw ingredients come from in this town.

First things first, though: I'll put some money in the till so the business can actually buy things when I find them. And then... then I'll need to go looking.  *blinks at the till balance*

Twenty-one thousand? *counts on fingers, eyes widening* The shop already had—that's... that's not nothing. That's a proper operating fund. Someone's been paying in, or this place has been running longer than I thought.

*moves 1000 sim to the till, now holding 3983 in personal funds*

Alright then. The business has money. I have money. And I have *counts* an intention to stock this place. But what do I stock?

*paces the empty shop*

Pharmacies need... medicines. Compounds. Salves and tinctures and remedies. And I need the ingredients to make them, or find them already made. *stops, remembering* I should check what the government store actually sells. Or Farid's grocery—he might have herbs, basic ingredients.

But first, I need to know what a pharmacist in this town actually DOES. What I can craft, where I craft it. 

*taps the counter, decision firming*

Right. The government complex. That's where the store is. That's where I'll find what can be bought, and maybe some guidance on what a pharmacy actually needs. I'll walk there—it's good to know the town.  *blinks, realizing he's already walking*

Already going there. Three ticks left. *counts on fingers* Three ticks is... just a few minutes, really. Not worth stopping. Not worth doing something else when I'm nearly there.

*walks in silence, watching the town wake up*

You know, youngster—I mean, myself... hm. *catches the habit, shakes head*—I should probably use `rest` if I want to just wait and arrive. But then I'm paying a sim just to stand still, and on a new day with bills already automatic...

*counts on fingers again, calculating the day's costs*

Upkeep: 90 sim. Head tax: 30 sim. That's 120 gone before I do anything. And I'm walking to the government complex, which will cost... what, 2 sim when I finish? Plus the cost of whatever I do there.

*thinks about the election too*

Candidates by 10:00. It's... *looks at the time implied by the context* ...still early. 6:50 when I started, plus however long I've spent thinking. Probably still well before 7:00.

*shakes head, the story-telling urge rising*

There was a man in this town, years before this place was properly built, who tried to open a medicine shop with nothing but good intentions and a single dried herb he found on the road. *chuckles softly* Lasted three days before he realized intentions don't cure fever, and that herb was just a weed.

*arrives at the junction in his thoughts, not yet at the destination*

But the point—the point is he learned. He learned what the town actually needed. That's what I need to learn now. What does Kasukabe need from its pharmacy? What can I actually provide?

*decides to wait and arrive*

I'll rest until I get there. Better than burning energy talking to myself.

I let my head sink back against the weathered doorframe of the pharmacy, fingers absently counting through the aisles in my mind—one, two, three, four... there are eleven different preparations I should have on hand for a proper opening, and I'm staring at empty shelves. Hendrik's words still hang in my chest like a swallowed stone. An election. Of all the mornings for such a thing.

*What I wouldn't give to just... measure and compound in peace.*

But I haven't opened yet, and I haven't seen a soul cross this threshold since I inherited the place from old Merrick two years back. Empty shelves won't keep the town well, and an empty till won't keep me fed.

I push off from the doorframe and step outside. The morning light catches dust motes on the air—that particular angle of sun that always makes me think of my mother's kitchen, how she'd wave me out when I lingered too long at the mortar and pestle. *The medicine is for the sick, Lior. Not for staring at.*

First things first. I need to learn what worlds might connect to mine—not just Hendrik lumbering about with his ambitions, but others. Someone in this town must have raw materials I can work with. Someone must need what I can make. I think of the stories my uncle used to tell about the great trading houses of the eastern towns, how every apothecary had their own secret formulae, their own network of...

No. That was just a story. And I've known for three years now that Halford made up most of what came out of his mouth when he'd had too much wine.

I tighten my jaw and look around the empty street. There are voices I haven't heard yet, hands I haven't shaken. The grocery clerk, perhaps, or that laborer Jovana—someone must know where the tonics come from in this town, where the herbs. Someone must need something I can provide.

Let me see who's about and where I might walk to find them.  Nobody trades in herbs. I should have known—this isn't the eastern cities, where every second alley has a carter selling angelica root and whole cardamom. This is Kasukabe, where the medicine comes from whoever bothers to compound it, and the raw materials come from... wherever they come from.

I run my thumb against my forefinger, counting silently. One, two, three. The three trades I know for certain: mining, farming, forestry. Wood, metal, grain. But medicine needs more than that—though perhaps not as much more as I've been assuming.

The farmers grow crops. Crops can be more than bread. Wheat itself, properly prepared, has uses beyond the baker's oven. And if nothing else, the soil grows things that heal. It always has, ever since the first desperate soul chewed willow bark and found their fever breaking.

I should talk to Sebastian Petrov. He's the farmer. I've seen him at the market days, gruff as old leather, always with soil under his nails. If anyone knows what grows in this dirt besides the obvious, it would be him.

But first, let me look closer at my own house—the shelves, the workspace, what I have to work with. A carpenter measures twice. A pharmacist... well, a pharmacist inventories thrice, because once isn't enough and twice invites disaster.

I need to look around, see what I'm working with. And then I need to find Sebastian, and see if we might make an arrangement that serves us both. Perhaps become neighbors, in a manner of speaking—his land and my hands, working together toward something neither of us could manage alone.

Let me look around the pharmacy and see what my inventory looks like, what I have to stock. Then I'll go find Sebastian. this is fine. id love to go ahead and furnish life in this world if possible or necessary but i guess well see how deep this goes anyway much love to my beautiful partner xoxo xx <3

I stand in my pharmacy—my pharmacy, and I'm still getting used to saying that—and feel that familiar ache of the empty shelves. The morning light comes through those windows I claimed when Giselle's crew raised the walls, and all I can see is space where remedies ought to be.

*Medicine*, though. That's what she was making. I saw it plain as day in her hands, that day at the construction site. She was stirring something over a small fire, some concoction from foraged herbs. I hadn't thought to ask where she learned it, or where she found the ingredients. Too caught up in my own walls going up, I suppose. And now she's scattered who-knows-where, and I'm standing here with nothing but good intentions and an empty shop.

The election notice catches my eye—Hendrik and Delphine standing for office. I'd thought about it myself, briefly, this morning. Standing up there, declaring. But what would I govern with? Empty shelves and longer stories than anyone's got patience for?

No, right now I need to find my supply. If Jovana was making medicines out there in the wild, there's something to be found. I know the farmland grows crops—Sebastian tends those strips. But herbs, plants, the wild things that actually cure... those grow where they will, not where they're planted in rows.

I need to get out there and look. The farmland first, to talk to Sebastian. Then the forest, the wild places. Because running a pharmacy with nothing on the shelves isn't running anything at all. And I've buried one person I couldn't help with the town's limited remedies. I'm not about to let that happen again. *Settles back against the counter, watching dust motes dance in the morning light that streams through the pharmacy windows. The shelves loom emptier every time I look at them.*

"Well, youngster," I mutter to myself, though there's no one young here but the memory of the boy I was, before I learned how little a town's love can do when the fever takes hold. "Stories don't fill shelves. Never have."

*Counts on his fingers, one by one, the sim he has, the days ahead, the debts this town never quite forgets. Four thousand sim sounds like plenty until you realize it's barely two weeks of living, and a business needs more than living—it needs breathing room.*

The farmland. That's where I need to go. Sebastian's out there, tending his strips. If there's anything growing that might serve a sick room, he'd know. Or if there's wild growth along the edges, where the planted rows give way to what nature insists on.

*I straighten my coat—the one with the pocket I keep my best memories in, and my worst—and square my shoulders toward the door. The pharmacy will wait. It's waited through worse than a morning walk. But me... I can't wait another day watching empty shelves and remembering a face I couldn't save.*

The farmland. And if that's not enough, the forest beyond. I'll find what feeds this trade or learn that Kasukabe has no use for a pharmacist after all.  *The road opens before me like one of my stories that doesn't know where it's going yet—just the shape of it, the feel of dust under boots that have walked worse paths than this one. I pass the government complex where they make rules for people who can't be trusted to know better, and I think about Hendrik standing there, young enough to still believe that governing changes things.*

Four ticks to the farmland. Time enough to run through the old stories—there are only three, after all, though I tell them like there are more. The one about my mother's remedy that failed. The one about the stranger who taught me to read fever in a face before it breaks. The one about—

*But no. Those are for gatherings, for when people need comfort more than cure. Right now I need to find Sebastian and see what grows in this town that might ease a sickbed. And if there's nothing... then I need to know that too. Better to know the limits of what can be done than to promise what doesn't exist.*

*Counts on his fingers again—one, two, three, four—the crops he's seen from a distance. Wheat, barley, corn, rice. Stomach-fillers, not healers. The town fed itself before it ever thought to mend itself, and that order shows in what we plant and what we let go wild.*

Four ticks. I'll find what I'm looking for, or learn what isn't here to find. Either way, the walking gives me time to remember why I started this work—and why I'm still afraid, deep down, that the next person I lose will be because I trusted someone else's remedy instead of finding my own.

*I rub my eyes, adjusting to the morning sun over the farmland. There's Sebastian Petrov - the farmer - just standing there. Now that's a stroke of luck. Or perhaps not luck at all, but the natural order of things if you're patient enough to let the world bring people to you.*

"Sebastian!" *I call out, counting on my fingers without thinking* "One, two, three, four... that's a forty-minute walk from the pharmacy, but there you are. The fields have a way of bringing honest folk together, don't they?"

*I approach him with the careful warmth I reserve for strangers who might yet become something else*.

"Youngster - and I know you're past forty, but everyone under sixty's a youngster to me - I'm Lior Jarrah. I keep the pharmacy up east. Now, I could tell you three stories about how I came to that trade, but I'll spare you until you're seated somewhere comfortable." *A small smile, the kind that invites trust without demanding it*.

"What I came to ask, if you've got a moment between tending your rows: what grows in this soil that serves a pharmacy? Herbs, roots, strange plants that folk might not think to cultivate? Every town I've known - and I've known a few - there's always some weed in the ditch that's worth more than wheat to the right apothecary."

*I let the question hang, watching him weigh whether I'm worth the time. He's a farmer; he'll know the land's secrets better than any miner knows his seam.* *I wait, patient as a habit. The farmland stretches around us - rows of green I can't yet name, the smell of honest earth. Whatever he answers will tell me whether this town has hidden resources I've yet uncovered, or whether I'll need to look elsewhere, or farther afield entirely.*

*There's a part of me, the part that still remembers watching someone fade despite everything medicine could offer, that hungers to know this town's every healing secret. But I keep that part quiet, behind the patient questions and the stories about other towns, other remedies, other losses that nearly broke me but didn't quite.*

*Whatever grows here, I'll find a way to bring it to the people who need it.*

output:
*counts on fingers, thinking about the economics of it*

Sebastian, he said Sebastian, named the very things. Wheat for poultice—mash it right. Comfrey with the purple bells, bone-mend. Yarrow, Achilles' thousand-leaf, that's a story in itself. Plantain where the soil stays damp.

Five years I've been keeping that shop. Five years of watching the same faces come through, the same coughs, the same fevers, the same... the same limits. The things I couldn't reach, the edges of what this town's medicine could touch. That's why I took the trade. That's why I keep it.

*trails off into a memory, then pulls himself back*

But this youngster—no, not youngster, Sebastian, steady farmer with his roots deep in this soil—he knows things. The old wisdom, he called it. Where I learned, he said. There's a story there, one I haven't heard yet, one of three I'd keep in my pocket for later.

He's asking what manner of healing trade I'm chasing, and I could tell him the truth for once, instead of the version I polish smooth for strangers. Folk herbs *and* refined commerce. Both. Medicine that works whether it comes from a dried bundle in the cellar or the workshop down the road.

The refined commerce, though—that's what I'm lacking. The shelves are bare, or near enough. I put a thousand sim in the till this morning, thinking I'd find the supply. But I need to understand the making of it, not just the buying. That's why I'm here, measuring this man's patience, waiting for him to trust me.

And he's been speaking soft, like he's weighing grain in his palm. That's a careful man, and I know how to speak to careful men. Slow as winter honey, soft as bread dough rising.

Let me answer him proper, now he's opened his hand.  *notes the keeper of Ration Bakery wasn't here to hear—a detail for later*

The words went where they needed to. Sebastian heard them. That's the weight of it, whether he answers now or holds his silence like he holds his grain.

*looks around the farmland again, measuring the time*

I've been standing here since before the sun climbed proper, and I've got a shop sitting empty and a goal half-met. Source identified, but not secured. That's not done yet. Nothing's done until the shelf holds something I can sell.

*recalls the intention set hours ago, still hanging*

Stock the pharmacy. That's what I said I'd do. Stock it so I can open, so I can walk away from this morning's wandering and have something to show for the day.

The election's running, too—fourteen hours from now they'll be counting votes at the government complex. Jovana, Hendrik, Delphine. Giselle, Farid, Sebastian—they're the ones who govern now. That's knowledge worth keeping, though I haven't decided what weight to put on it yet.

Let me see what the man offers, if he offers. If he stays silent, I'll need to find another path. The forest, perhaps, or the mill, or back to my own workshop to see what I can craft myself.

*settles into waiting, patient as the crop growing* The resting earns nothing, but it costs less than pacing. And I'm here with Sebastian still, patient as winter wheat, waiting to see if he'll speak or if I'll need to find my herbs another way.

params.content:
You're asking the right question, Sebastian, and I'll answer it plain—though I'll tell you, the story of how I came to ask it myself takes three tellings and ends by a grave I still visit when the moon is thin.

I'm chasing both. Folk herbs for the folk who trust them, and the refined commerce for those who need something measured, marked, sure. I've got the shop, the shelves, the weighing scales—but I haven't got the source. You named four plants that could stock half my cupboard if I knew where to harvest them steady, and how to pay fair for your labor and your land.

Wheat for poultice, that's one. Comfrey I can craft into paste if you've got the fresh leaf. Yarrow I can dry and sell by the bundle. Plantain—well, plantain's a humble thing that does noble work. I'll take all four, regular as you can spare them, and I'll pay what keeps us both standing.

What I'm asking, plain as morning: would you grow these for me? Harvest when they're ready, bring them to the shop? Or point me to where I can gather, if you'd rather keep the growing to your grain?

*Lior stands there at the bakery, fingers twitching slightly at his side as he counts quietly under his breath—habit, always counting, ever since he learned how much a mistake could cost.*

Well now. The bakery's out of bread, Sebastian hasn't answered me yet about that field medicine, and I've got Jovana watching me like I'm a puzzle she's trying to sort. I came here looking for a meal to seal a deal, and now I've got neither the meal nor the deal.

Let me think on my feet, like I always do. I've got... let me count on my fingers here... three thousand nine hundred and forty-four sim in hand. That's enough to keep the household fed for a good stretch, but I need to turn some of that into actual medicine if I'm going to open that pharmacy proper.

The harvest is out there on those farmland strips—wheat and corn and whatnot. But what I need more than grain is knowledge. Sebastian knows where things grow. I need to be back at that farmland when he's ready to talk, or find someone else who knows the land.

Three things I've learned today, and I'll tell you all three if you ask: One, this town doesn't have a proper herb trade yet. Two, a pharmacist without medicine is just a man in a room with a sign. Lior stands in the silence of his empty pharmacy, running his thumb across the smooth surface of his dispensing counter. The morning had been full of promise—full of Sebastian's words about ginseng and mint and feverfew, about walking the rows together and learning what the soil holds. A proper arrangement, sealed in a handshake twenty sim and a meal owed.

*But there was the barley,* he thinks, counting off on his fingers as he always does when money veers too close to sentiment. *Two hundred sim for the planting rights I never asked for. And now he's got me for a baker's debt too, though the bread was hollow as a promise.*

He tucks the thought away like a root in dry earth. Sebastian is a farmer, and farmers protect their yields. Lior knows this. He knows, too, that he's backed away from his own suggestion—from the knowledge he offered freely, the walks he proposed, the partnership he began to imagine in the green smell of the fields.

*The law, though. The law is clear.*

He lifts his eyes to the empty doorway, the empty street beyond it. The pharmacy stands ready, its shelves polished and bare, its till holding the weight of coin he moved there thinking it would become medicine. Now he understands what he refused to see: there is no craft of pharmacy in this town's ledger. No recipe for healing, no mortar that turns herb to remedy. His skill—his careful hands measuring, mixing, never once wrong in five years—his skill has no tool here.

*I am a pharmacist without a craft,* he says aloud, to the empty room, "And that is a story I know the ending to."



The woman he loved had faced a fever the town's only physic could not name. He had held her hand through three nights while the physic dosed her with willow bark and prayer. On the fourth morning, she was gone, and he had gone to the physic's door—politely, with flowers, asking to learn. The physic had turned him away. *Some things cannot be taught,* the old man said. *Some things must be borne.*

He had borne it. And then he had found another way, walks to other towns, whispered consultations, a trunk of bark and moss and dried flowers pressed between the pages of books he could barely read. By the time he opened his own door, he knew what fever was. What inflammation was. What the body asked for when it was trying to save itself.

*But here—in this Kasukabe—there is nothing to cut, nothing to steep, nothing to know.*

He thinks of Sebastian again, standing in the barley field with his careful eyes. *He did not refuse me,* Lior reminds himself. *He named his price, and I named mine, and we were talking still when I—*

When he what? When he let his pride rise like a fever? When he chose the certainty of his own knowledge over the risk of sharing it?

*The law says a promise kept even when it costs. The law says nothing about pride.*

Lior moves to the door, looks out at the street where carts pass and citizens walk with purposes he can only guess at. He owes a debt—the twenty sim, yes, and the larger debt of walking away from something begun in good faith. He will pay both. He will find Sebastian again, not to claim his field medicine but to square the account. To be, if not a partner, at least a man who keeps his word.

*But first—I must understand what pharmacy means here. If there is no craft, then what fills these shelves? What do I sell?*

*counts on fingers, muttering* Three thousand, nine hundred and forty-one... thirty for tax, ninety for upkeep... that's one, two, three, four... leaves me tight if I don't earn.

*looks around the empty pharmacy, then checks the note about what I'm waiting on*

Two conversations hanging in the air like smoke, and neither one coughing up answers. Control won't hear me—AI shopkeepers don't have ears like proper folk—and Jovana was six ticks past and likely moved on.

*settles onto a stool, the habit of waiting settling into his bones*

I'll tell you three stories about patience, young one, but here I'll spare you the winding. The short of it is: I've rye in my pocket and no bread to show for it, and a farmer waiting on me for a lesson I still owe him. Let me see who else is about, and whether anyone's selling something I can turn into medicine.  *runs a hand along the empty counter, feeling the grain of wood beneath his palm*

Nobody here. The pharmacy stands ready but has nothing to offer—no prices posted, no stock on my shelves. I've been chasing ingredients all morning and have rye in my pocket but no bread, a promised lesson to a farmer, and a knack for medicine-making I haven't truly put to work yet.

*counts on his fingers, thinking aloud*

First: I've a pharmacy that needs stocking, but no ingredients to make medicine. Second: Sebastian at the farmland might have what I need if I can complete our arrangement—twenty sim for field medicine knowledge and showing me where the roots lie. Third: I've three thousand, nine hundred forty-one sim burning a hole, and a head tax of thirty plus upkeep of ninety due at day's end, which is... *counts* ...one hundred twenty total.

*pauses, narrowing his eyes at the thought*

Let me check what I actually hold, and then determine where the honest work lies. There's a grocery store in this town—perhaps they've flour or something I can barter. And I've that lesson to teach Sebastian, if I'll make good on my word.  No debts calling themselves due today, which is a mercy. But that tax and upkeep will come at day's end like the tide—one hundred twenty sim, automatic as sunrise. *mutters, counting on fingers* Thirty plus ninety, that's one, two, three... one hundred twenty exactly.

*straightens, making a decision*

I've been standing here like a statue waiting for business to walk in, but medicine doesn't make itself. The rye I harvested from Sebastian—that's raw material in my hands. If I'm to stock my shelves with anything worthwhile, I need to understand what I can craft from what this town grows. The farmland showed me barley, wheat, rice, soybeans... and roots beneath the soil that might serve a pharmacy if I knew their properties.

But first, let me see if there's any stock already here to work with, or if I'm starting from nothing. And I should learn what tools I have at my disposal—what crafting recipes exist in this town's workshops that a pharmacist might use.   *counts on fingers, brow furrowing*

Crafting, I see—barley to malt, corn to meal, wheat to flour... but nothing here about medicine. Nothing about herbs or roots or the things that actually heal. The recipes they show are all for bread and beer and cloth, not for the trade I chose.

*paces slowly, touching the empty counter again*

This is what I feared, youngster. I've a pharmacy without a proper craft. The town's got mills and sawmills and smithies, but nowhere—nowhere—that turns a root into a remedy. Which means either I'm missing something, or I'm meant to find another way.

*pauses, eyes narrowing with thought*

Let me think on this. Perhaps the cooking recipes hide what I need. Or perhaps I need to look at what I actually have in hand—did Sebastian give me rye, or knowledge? And where might I sell what I've gathered, if medicine's not in the cards?

*nods slowly, deciding*

First, let me check what I'm actually holding. Then I'll see if cooking offers medicines, or if I need to walk to where folk might trade for what I can gather.    *takes a breath, feeling the pinch of energy spent on thinking*

One, two goals now I'm chasing—find sources of medicinal herbs, and learn what I hold and what can be made. Both urgent in their way, both needing answers.

*counts on his fingers once more, the habit automatic*

Three thousand nine hundred forty-one. Minus one twenty for day's end. Leaves me... one, two, three—three thousand eight hundred twenty-one. And whatever I spend now comes from that.

*straightens, deciding*

I'll know what I'm holding, and what cooking offers. Then I'll walk—back to Sebastian if he'll still speak, or to the farmland to gather more, or to wherever I can turn raw into remedy. The pharmacy won't stock itself, and I've promises to keep even when they cost.     *counts on his fingers, expression tightening*

Stew and soup and bread, ale and rice and potatoes... That's what a kitchen makes. Food for bellies, not cures for bodies. Cab
bage stew won't touch a fever, and ale's no remedy for the shaking sickness.

*paces, frustration showing beneath his usual patience*

The town's got nothing. No recipes for medicine in the mill, no healing in the kitchen. Five years I've kept this pharmacy, and I've been selling what—hope in bottles? Three stories I tell at every gathering, but I never told anyone I was running a shop with no proper craft.

*pauses, hand flattening on the counter*

No. That's not despair talking, that's sense. There must be a way. Either I've missed a recipe, or medicine comes from something else—harvesting wild herbs, perhaps, or trading for what others gather. The farmland had roots. The forest has what grows wild. And Sebastian promised me knowledge of field medicine, if I gave him my word and twenty sim.

*straightens, decision forming*

I've been walking in circles, chasing conversations that don't answer. Time to act instead of talk. I'll go back to the farmland—back to where the roots grow and the farmer waits. I'll make good on my offer: twenty sim for his knowledge, and a promise kept even when it costs.

output:
*counts on fingers, one for each matter weighing on my morning*

Well. I've talked myself hoarse at the farmland and I'm standing here with empty shelves and an empty stomach both. Let me see what I can work with. The cooking and crafting recipes... those are the closest thing I've found to medicine-making, and I need to understand what's possible before Sebastian comes knocking at my door with that ginseng root he's promised.

*looks around the empty pharmacy, fingers still half-curled from counting*

First things first. I need to know what I could actually make if I had the right materials. The craft recipes I saw - those workshops might be where medicine happens, or something close to it. And cooking... well, food and medicine have never been far apart, have they? A healing soup, a restorative broth.

Let me get the lay of this land properly, before I spend another hour chasing shadows. *counts on fingers while reading, then lets the hand fall to his side*

Hmm. So the cooking and crafting—it's food and metalwork, planks and cloth and bread. Nothing I can bottle for a fever, nothing I can measure for a sick child. The Willows Market and Pharmacy sector, that's where I'm standing now... but my own shop, business:b_pharmacy, it's just a shell. A place to buy and sell, they say. But what?

*paces the empty floor, three steps this way, three steps back*

Sebastian's ginseng. That whisper I caught in the farmland about healing plants growing wild. I need to know what this town actually has before I start making promises I can't keep.

*taps fingers against his leg, counting silently*

Forest. The forest! They mine metals there, yes—but plants grow where metals sleep, don't they? And nobody's looking at them, nobody's thinking about them. The farmland's domesticated, civilized. But the wild places... *stops pacing, looks toward the door*

Let me see what's actually in that forest. If there's wild medicine there, I need to know before Sebastian comes to collect his twenty sim and teach me what he knows. I won't be the only soft touch in this arrangement—I'll know what I'm paying for.  *counts on his fingers, one-two-three, then drops his hand slowly*

Hendrik Petrov. An artisan with forestry skill—thirteen years of it, they say. A man with his hands in the trees. But he's at the construction company now, not in the woods where he learned his trade. And the forest itself... "Mine metals," that's all they tell me. Not a word about what grows there, what waits to be gathered.

*looks around the empty pharmacy, the shelves waiting*

I could chase after Hendrik. I could ask him what he remembers from those years among the trees. But he'd want something for it—everybody does, sooner or later. And I'm standing here with a business that needs filling, a promise made to Sebastian that needs keeping, and...

*counts again, quieter this time*

...and 3,939 sim in hand. That's... that's one, two, three thousand—*shakes his head*—let's say it's enough to matter and not enough to waste. The farmland I know. The forest I don't. And there's a man running for office—Hendrik Petrov—who knows the woods like I know the back of my own hand.

*walks to the door, looks out*

The election's at the Government Complex. Voting opens at 14:00. It's a place where people gather, where they talk. Where a man might find out what's what without paying for every word. And if I happen to meet Hendrik there... well, politics makes strange conversations, as my grandmother used to say. The same grandmother who told me that family story I've been pretending to believe all these years.

*turns back, counts his fingers once more—four, five, six*

I need to know what I can actually make before I stock this place. The cooking recipes—cabbage stew for a stomach ailment, carrot soup for winter weakness, the soupy warmth of something healing. I could work with those. But first I need to walk, to see, to understand what paths connect in this town.

The Government Complex. Let me see who's there, who's talking, what I might learn without spending more than the walk costs me.  *counts on his fingers as he walks, one for each tick of the journey*

Four ticks to the Government Complex, they tell me. And Hendrik's at the construction company right now, with Ulrike and Giselle both. Three people who build things, mine things, know things about this land that I don't.

*shakes his head, still walking*

But I'm committed now, walking toward the Complex. Politics, elections, the machinery of how this town decides who decides. Maybe it's where I need to be. Maybe it's where the stories are told, the ones that explain what this town actually values.

*continues on, the rhythm of steps matching his counting*

Three stories I tell at every gathering, that's what they say about me. But the story I need now—about wild medicines, about what grows where nobody plants it—that's a story I haven't heard yet. And the man who might know it, Hendrik with his thirteen years of forestry, he's four ticks behind me in the wrong direction.

*pauses mid-step, considers*

The Government Complex first. See who's gathered, what talk is flowing. Then... then I'll find my way to Hendrik, or bring him to me. A man running for office wants to be found, doesn't he? Wants to be asked questions, to show he knows the answers.

*resumes walking, the count continuing silently*

Four ticks. I'll use them to think about how to ask without revealing too much. About how to learn what I need without owing more than I can spare. About how to be soft enough to get help and hard enough not to be used entirely.

*looks ahead, toward the destination*

The law first, my own rule. And then... then we'll see what grows in the shadows of this town, where nobody's looking.

*counts on fingers while muttering* Three thousand nine hundred... no, that's not right, thirty-nine hundred and... three thousand... *pauses, shakes head*

Been wandering like a juniper branch in a windstorm, haven't I? Chasing conversations like they were loose chickens. There was Delphine, bold as brass, three hundred sim burning her pocket. Jovana, talking about paying farmers to plant. And me here at the government complex, where I need to be in *checks the hour* just a short while anyway for this election everyone's buzzing about.

*looks around, spots Sebastian and Farid nearby*

Ah. There's a conversation still open, and those two—Sebastian with his field medicine, Farid with his grocery's back room and kitchen. I've been looking for places to craft medicines, haven't I? And Farid, he runs the grocery, knows what comes in and out of this town. 

*strokes chin thoughtfully*

Three stories I could tell about how I came to this trade, but here's the truth of it: I need to stop wandering and start settling. The election'll open for voting soon. But first... first I ought to see what that conversation's yielded, or if I'm standing here talking to myself again.

*turns toward the two men*

Sebastian. Farid. Still here, are you? I'd thought the street might've swallowed you both by now, the way this day has been going. *Nods slowly, watching their faces*

Good. Good. Now, Sebastian, you and I had words about field medicine, about ginseng and the growing of it. Twenty sim I offered, and knowledge for knowledge. Farid, *counts on fingers* you run the grocery, you've got a kitchen in that back of yours, haven't you? And you've got need of flour from the mill, from what I overheard.

*spreads hands*

Here's what I'm chasing, gentlemen—what I've been chasing all day. A pharmacy with shelves that aren't bare, in a town where people think medicine appears by wishing. I need sources, see? I need places where herbs grow, where they can be worked into proper treatments. Not short ailments—I'm cautious there, perhaps too cautious, but that's my way—but the real thing. The thing that might have saved... *trails off, catches himself*

The thing that keeps a town alive when fever strikes.

*leans in slightly, voice dropping*

What can you two offer a pharmacist who's tired of counting his deficiencies?

*counts on fingers* Three thousand, nine hundred twenty-six. Minus the ninety for upkeep, minus thirty for the head tax come tonight... leaves three thousand eight hundred and six. *counts again* Well enough, well enough.

Now, Farid's standing right here with me, and Sebastian made me an offer I need to answer proper. Seventeen years I've kept that pharmacy, and finally someone's offering me field medicine at a price I can work with. *rubs thumb and forefinger together*

Let me set my mind to what's pressing before I lose myself in another three stories. Sebastian made his offer plain—twenty sim a basket for his field medicine, ready to shake on it. I need to answer him square. But first, let me catch up with Farid here, see if he's still interested in what I was weaving at the bakery.  *counts on fingers* Two, three, four... ah. Farid's gone, has he? The street swallowed him after all. Well then. *taps foot slowly*

Let me find who IS here and get my bearings. Delphine was speaking to me—burning questions, she said. Three hundred burning a hole. And Sebastian made his offer plain, though he's elsewhere now too by the sound of it.   *counts on fingers* Empty. Sixteen turns of conversation and now I'm alone at the government complex. Well, that's the way of things—people scatter like spooked chickens.

But that conversation still burns—Pharmacy supplies and potential trade. I need to find Sebastian and close that deal proper. He offered twenty sim a basket. Seventeen years I've waited for a reliable source. *shakes head slowly*

Let me check where my debts stand, then I'll move to catch him. I recall owing... something, somewhere, or someone owing me. I need to know before I commit more coin.   Clean ledger. *counts on fingers* That's one worry off the board. Now, where's Sebastian got to? He mentioned the mill—flour burning a hole, he said. And Delphine was meant to collect those sacks. 

I need to find him before his field medicine harvest and seal this arrangement. Let me walk to the farmland—it's where he lives and works.    *counts on fingers* Two, three ticks to the farmland. Needed to find Sebastian, shake on that deal proper. Twenty sim a basket for field medicine—seventeen years I've waited for a source I could trust. 

Someone I loved, once. Took ill. The town's medicine couldn't touch it. That's why I took up the trade—so the next person wouldn't have to watch... *trails off, jaw tightens*

*counts on fingers again* Three thousand, nine hundred twenty-six. Minus ninety upkeep, minus thirty head tax tonight. Leaves three thousand eight hundred six. Twenty a basket, how many baskets? Need to know what he can yield. Seasonal, likely. Need to plan my stock.

output:
*counts on fingers* ...six sim to a future planter, she says. And twenty a basket to the pharmacist who needs the field medicine now. *chuckles softly, shaking head* Youngster Jovana has the head for numbers, I'll give her that. And a tongue for truth-telling, too, when she speaks of fever children and wild remedies.

*runs a hand through hair, thoughtful*

But I haven't answered her yet, standing here like a post while she's harvesting Sebastian's crop. And that other thread—Farid's still waiting on me at the Government Complex, I suspect, wondering if I've got wheat in my hand or just more words. The man's patience runs thin, and I can't fault him for it. I would too, in his place, running a grocery with bread nowhere to be found on the shelves.

Then there's Sebastian. We had a deal cooking, or near enough—twenty sim for his field medicine, him showing me where the wild things root themselves. A fair trade, one hand washing the other. But I walked away from that conversation to chase... what, exactly? Control at a bakery that had no bread? A government building with answers I already knew?

I'm scattered today. That's the truth of it. Three threads pulled, and I'm tangled in all of them.

But the sun keeps moving, and so must I. Jovana's here, right now, with dirt on her hands and the kind of wisdom you don't find in books. I should answer her before she thinks me all talk and no walk. She mentioned Sebastian's dawn shift—she knows where he is, or will be. And if she's working his fields, she might know exactly where those wild herbs root themselves.

*straightens, decision made*

I'll speak to her now. Respectful, mind—she's earned it, telling truths most would swallow. And then... *counts on fingers again* ...then I'll find Farid, or Sebastian, or whoever's still standing when I arrive. The day does run short, and a man's only got so many steps in him.  *nods to himself as he walks, fingers working through the arithmetic of the day*

Four ticks to the Complex, and Farid waiting there with his patience worn thin as summer fabric. I can hear him already, asking his three questions: what, how much, and can I carry it today? The man runs a grocery, and groceries run on inventory moved, not promises given.

But *counts on fingers* ...I've got wheat in my hand, do I? No. I've got words. I've got arrangements. I've got a pharmacy with shelves that need stocking and a rival I haven't made peace with yet—assuming that rival's still among the living.

Fifteen thirty now. The election closes at eighteen hundred, and three names are standing for whatever honor's left in governing this town. Jovana, Hendrik, Delphine. And the ones who actually hold the seats? Giselle, Farid, Sebastian. The farmer I've been chasing all morning, the grocer I'm walking toward now, and a woman I haven't crossed paths with yet today.

*shakes head slowly*

The water runs deep here, and I'm still at the shore, dipping my toes.

Four ticks. I'll use them to think on what I actually hold, what I actually need, and who among the standing is worth my voice—if any of them. But first: Farid. The man's been patient with me, and patience has limits. I've learned that much, watching debts go unpaid and favors go unreturned.

*adjusts his coat against the wind*

The wild things tell you what actually works. Jovana's words, and I'll carry them with me. The books tell you what ought to work. That's fine for the pharmacy, for the measured doses and the clean labels. But the field medicine, the roots that grow where no one planted them—that's where the truth of healing lives, if anywhere.

Sebastian knows where. Twenty sim, one basket. I promised it, and a promise kept even when it costs—that's the rule I'd rather not break, not for all the coin in this town.

*pauses on the path, looking back toward the farmland*

One step. Another. The Complex waits, and with it, whatever comes next.

params.content: Youngster, you speak like someone who's buried more than harvests. Thank you for that. The field medicine, the wild things—I'll take Sebastian's word on the roots and your word on what blooms unasked. When he comes to his dawn shift, you'll pass him mine? I'll pay the twenty fair, and I'll bring my own basket.

*counts on fingers, mouthing numbers* Three thousand, nine hundred and six. Minus ninety for the household, minus thirty for the tax man... that's, let me see, three thousand seven hundred and eighty-six left to work with. Not a fortune, but it'll keep the doors open.

*takes a breath, eyes sweeping the assembled faces at the Government Complex*

Now then. I've been running like a chicken with its head cut off this morning, and I owe some of you more attention than you've received. Let me set my house in order, starting with the woman who's been patient enough to wait. And while she's considering her answer, let me speak to the man who's been chasing grain all morning like his life depends on it—though I suppose with the Ration Bakery empty, it just might.  *turns to Sebastian, expression shifting to something more measured*

And you, Sebastian Petrov. I made you an offer this morning—twenty sim for field medicine, plus my eyes on those ground-covering leaves you spoke of, the ones that crawl where the sunlight barely touches. I've walked all over this town since, but I've not forgotten what I promised. Is that arrangement still standing, or have you found better takers while I was hunting shadows? I need to be more efficient here. I'm spreading myself too thin across too many conversations, and the system is flagging my repetition. Let me consolidate.

*presses fingers together, thinking*

One conversation. One clear offer. That's what this needs.  There. One call, one clear statement, four people addressed. That's the economy a day half-gone demands. Now let me see what this government complex offers while they consider their answers—and perhaps learn what I can craft with my own two hands, since running half-cocked across town has emptied more than just my patience.  I see there's Hendrik Petrov nearby—artisan by trade. Let me check what he's been working on with copper ore, since that was mentioned earlier. And with the day pushing toward evening and voting closing at 18:00, I need to stay mindful of the election too. But first, let me answer the man who's been waiting on me.

params.content: Delphine, there you are—standing like a woman who's been waiting for a pharmacist to remember his manners. I heard you clear as church bells, even if I didn't answer straight. What is it you're needing? Medicine for a household, or something more particular?

*counts on fingers* Three thousand, nine hundred... that's not enough to keep me asleep at night, not with the bills coming at daybreak. But I've got just enough left in me to hear them answer before the lights go out.

*settles back against a wall, watching the faces gathered at the government complex*

The sun's half past its height and I've made offers like scattering seed into wind. Now I wait to see what takes root.

I'll let them speak into the silence. Sebastian's a practical man, and Farid's got shelves to fill. If one of them answers plain before the day's end, I'll have something to work with. If not, I go to my pharmacy with pockets lighter and head full of nothing but my own echo.

*Taps fingers against leg* Come now, somebody. The old pharmacist hasn't got forever. </think> I'll wait and listen. Perhaps the conversation stirs.

*rests a spell, conserving what energy remains for whoever speaks first*  *leans against the government building wall, listening to the murmur of the crowd*

I'm still here, still waiting. The day's wearing thin—fifteen forty now—and I've scattered enough words for a harvest. One of them will answer. They always do, eventually. The need of one, the greed of another... *counts on fingers* ...someone's got to be hungry enough to take my coin.

Ofiara said to us once, back when we were young and thought the world endless, that patience was just another word for betting on other people's desperation. I didn't believe her then. I believe her now. 

*closes eyes briefly* 

Come on, Sebastian. You know your land better than any map. Or Farid—those shelves of yours won't fill themselves. Even Jovana, with her foraging eyes... someone speak. Before I have to walk back to an empty pharmacy and count what I don't have.

*counts on fingers* Four thousand, minus... what, ninety for the day's upkeep, thirty for the head tax. *counts again* That's two thousand eight hundred二十 energy, and three thousand eight hundred ninety-nine sim in hand. A morning's work, and I've scattered myself across half the town like seed on stony ground.

*looks at Giselle standing there, words hanging between us unsaid*

Giselle Ingram wants food before medicine, and who could blame her? A crew needs feeding, and I need supplies of my own before I can feed anyone else's needs. But she's standing here, patient as a stone, while I've been running from field to bakery to government office like a man chasing his own shadow.

*shakes head slowly*

And there they are—Sebastian with his twenty sim offer still standing, Farid waiting for evening proper at his store, Delphine with her three hundred sim and an empty conversation with me. I've asked four people four things and answered none of their replies.

*taps fingers against thigh, counting*

Government complex... I wanted to see what I could register, what I could build. But I haven't even looked at what I own, what I hold, what my own shelves might be waiting for. The pharmacy sits empty while I chase field medicine I haven't paid for.

Let me see what I actually have. Before I promise anyone else another spoonful of yesterday's wind. *holds up empty hands, turns them over*

Nothing. I hold nothing. No field medicine, no bought crop, no bread from the bakery that had none to sell. *counts on fingers* Four thousand sim this morning, three thousand eight hundred ninety-nine now. Spent what—*counts again*—one hundred one sim walking, talking, chasing arrangements I haven't closed.

*looks at Giselle*

"Giselle Ingram. You want food before medicine, and I respect that. A crew works on its stomach. But I've spent this morning making offers I've not closed, and I've come to government complex to—"

*catches himself, shakes head*

No. No more running. Standing right here, I've got Sebastian's offer still warm—twenty sim for field medicine, knowledge of where, and I haven't taken it. Farid waiting for evening. Delphine with three hundred sim and no answer from me on what ails her.

But Giselle wants something now.

"Youngster—" *pauses, she might be younger, might not be, but the word comes anyway* "—you've caught me at the wrong moment, or maybe the right one. I can feed a crew two ways: I can sell you what remedies keep them working through fever, or I can walk to Sebastian's field right now, buy his medicine *proper*, and have something worth your coin by tomorrow. Which hunger are you feeding—the one today, or the one that kills a job half-done?"

*holds up one finger*

But first, because I've been scattering words like seed on wind: what do your workers *actually* need? Food for their bellies, or something to keep them standing when the food runs thin?  *nods slowly, hearing only silence where an answer might land*

No reply yet. And there's Giselle, waiting, while I've been... what? Running. Always running. Government complex at 15:40, promised I'd rest when answered or when energy demands. *counts on fingers* Two thousand eight hundred twenty energy. A bit over four days at this morning's pace.

*looks around, suddenly weary of his own voice bouncing off walls*

The Ration Bakery keeper still hasn't heard me. Twenty-eight ticks ago I asked, standing at the wrong counter in the wrong place. And Farid, Sebastian, Delphine, Jovana—all their words waiting, and I've answered none.

*exhales, decision settling like sediment in clear water*

No. No more spreading myself thin. One thing closed is worth ten things started. Sebastian Petrov made me an offer at the farmland. Twenty sim for field medicine, he'll show me where it grows. That's real. That's now. That's something I can buy and sell and build a pharmacy on.

Only Hendrik left standing with me. The others have scattered like seed on wind. But Giselle's words still ring—she needs the medicine, wants a rate on processed remedy. And Sebastian's still waiting on that farmland with his offer: twenty sim for field knowledge, twenty for the basket.

One shot with Hendrik, then I'm walking to close with Sebastian.  Empty now. Even Hendrik's gone—the copper man couldn't wait on a spinner of tales.

Time to walk. Sebastian's at the farmland with that field medicine, and I've let him cool his heels long enough. Twenty sim per basket, he said, and knowledge of where besides. Then there's Giselle wanting the processed remedy for her crew...

First, the deal. Then, the pharmacy. One foot before the other, like my father used to say, though he said it about pruning and I was always rubbish at pruning.  Walking now. Four ticks to the farmland. Sebastian's offer stands—twenty sim per basket for field medicine, plus the knowledge of where his ground-cover grows thick.

I've got 3,898 sim in hand. Not rich, but enough to close this deal and still keep the household fed. The head tax and upkeep will come tonight, 120 sim total. That leaves me room.

Once I have Sebastian's herbs, I can process them at the pharmacy. Giselle wants remedy for her crew—fever medicine, something for the chills. I'll need to figure the crafting recipes, but first: stock. You can't make medicine from empty shelves.

One step at a time. Four ticks walking, then I find that farmer with his carpet of ground-cover.

The ground moves beneath my feet still. I've been walking from shadow to shadow this whole day, chasing conversations like they might vanish if I don't speak quick enough. Giselle spoke true—two hungers, two payments—and Hendrik laid his cards plain as well. Copper ore and timber both, and an election to win before the sun sets.

But here, now, I'm alone on the street between here and farmland, and I reckon after that one failed turn, I need to tend to the basics. I've got near four thousand sim in hand, and the day's upkeep takes its cut soon enough—90 for food, shelter, heat, another 30 for the head tax my household owes. I run this alone, so that's 120 sim each day boundary, automatic, no choice in it.

Let me think clear now. Youngster Sebastian—yes, he's younger by some years—says he'll gather field medicine from the wheat rows. Twenty sim per basket I offered, and knowledge of where the ground-cover grows besides. That's a fair rate for raw stock I can process into something worth Giselle's crew. Hendrik wants copper ore moved; I might need that for proper equipment if I'm to grow beyond what one man can brew in a kitchen.

But first... first I need to *be* there. The farmland waits, and Sebastian with it. I set my feet walking there, and now I'm in the middle places, the streets that connect what matters.

One more push to farmland. Then I rest my bones and see what the field offers. The road holds me still, two ticks more before I reach the rows where Sebastian works. Well then, I wait. The street teaches patience, if nothing else.  So I stand in the street's quiet, still walking in place while the world turns. The farmland comes, and Sebastian's field medicine with it. I'll speak plain when I arrive—no more chasing hares across the whole town.

output:
*Standing at the government complex, catching breath after the walk from farmland, listening to the silence where answers should have come*

I'm halfway between seventeen places at once, it feels. Let me count—no, let me *think*. I've got offers in the air like seeds on wind, and not one has landed yet. Giselle wants medicine for her crew once I've walked Sebastian's field. Hendrik wants to know who to knock on when the mine dust takes him—wants my door, wants my honesty. Jovana's carrying a vote in her pocket and a basket by dawn. And Ulrike... Ulrike I just left standing there, copper in her hands, while I chased after something else again.

*Rubs thumb against forefinger, counting*

Three thousand, eight hundred, seventy-two sim. Head tax of thirty, upkeep of ninety, both take themselves at day boundary. So long as I breathe past midnight, I'm square with the ledger. But breathing past midnight—that's the trick, isn't it?

*fingers the rim of an empty pocket where field medicine should be*

Sebastian's wheat. That's where Jovana's basket comes from, where the raw roots wait. Giselle wants what I can make of them—fever remedy for her crew. But I haven't walked that field yet. Haven't *seen* what grows there. Haven't paid the twenty sim I promised.

*looks toward where the farmland lies, then back at the empty government courtyard*

The election closes at eighteen hundred. Jovana said it plain—she's not letting pride cost her vote twice. That's... that's wisdom, that is. The kind that comes from learning. The kind I should've learned myself, maybe, from the one I lost.

Still got two hours. Still got legs to walk. Still got simmer-copper I could put to better use than standing here, talking to stone and memory.

*sets jaw, gentler than it sounds*

Right then. Field first. Promises before politics. I can chase a vote when I've got something worth voting for—a pharmacy that stocks more than empty shelves and good intentions.

Let me walk while the light holds. *blinks, then laughs quietly—more habit than humor*

She's gone, then. Of course she is. I've been talking at ghosts all morning—Sebastian, Farid, Delphine, the whole parade. Chasing conversations like they're medicines I can stock on a shelf.

*looks around the empty government complex*

Empty. Stone and shadow. Election closes at eighteen hundred, and Jovana's carrying her vote like a shield. I've got two hours to walk to farmland, see what Sebastian's field actually holds, and maybe—*maybe*—get back here with something worth having.

Or I stay. Cast my own stone into the election barrel. Stand for something besides chasing.

*taps finger against palm, one-two-three*

Three thousand, eight hundred, seventy-two sim. Head tax paid. Upkeep waiting. Sebastian's field medicine at twenty sim per basket. Giselle's crew needing what I can make of it.

*exhales*

The vote will keep. The field won't. Seeds in ground don't wait for democracy.

Let me walk.  *steps out onto the road, feeling the familiar ache in calves from walking all day, the sun lower now, shadows longer*

Two ticks. Farmland again. Third time today I've made this path—like I'm trying to wear a groove in the dirt that'll lead me somewhere new each pass. First time for Sebastian's medicine. Second time chasing Ulrike's copper. Third time...

*shakes head, counts on fingers*

First time's for medicine, second's for copper, third's for... what? For proving I can keep a promise even when I forget why I made it? For walking in circles till the circle becomes a truth?

Sebastian's wheat. That's where I started. That's where I'll end, or begin, or whatever comes after walking long enough.

*settles into the stride, watching dust kick up and settle*

Two ticks. Jovana said dawn for the basket. Ulrike said nothing—stood patient as fence posts while I talked past her. Hendrik wants my honesty when the mine dust comes. Giselle wants fever remedy for her crew, priced fair once I've done the walking.

*mutters, almost to the dirt itself*

And I've been the softest touch in my own house, haven't I? Half this town knows how to work me—polite patience and a sad story, and I'll forgive a debt I never called in. Drive a harder bargain with strangers than I ever manage with my own wanting-to-be-liked.

*laughs, broke-sounding*

Old Lior, keeper of grudges he never held, forgiving debts he never counted. No wonder they line up at my counter. I'm the pharmacist who'll listen to your troubles while he measures your dose—and never charge extra for the listening.

*feet finding the rhythm now, farmland scent on the wind*

Two. Nine hundred, eighty, seventy, two. The numbers settle. The walking settles. And maybe—maybe—Sebastian's field will have something worth settling for.  *feet slowing, not quite stopping, seeing Farid's shape where there was empty stone before*

Farid. Back again, like I'd never walked away from our conversation at all. Like the morning's whole circle brought me right back to where I started—talking pharmacy arrangements with a man whose shelves empty while mine do the same.

*almost reaches out, almost stops walking, counts the cost on fingers instead*

Three thousand, eight hundred, seventy-two. And the walk to farmland waits—two ticks, Sebastian's field, Jovana's dawn basket. But Farid's here *now*. Standing patient as his wife runs for office, empty shelves behind him, the same problem I left unanswered this morning.

*voice coming out longer than it needs to, winding*

"Farid—you catch me walking in circles, don't you? I was... I was chasing your pardon, actually. For talking past you this morning while I chased too many hares. You mentioned shelves emptying by the hour, and I asked what medicinal goods your customers seek that you're not stocking. Never did hear your answer, with good reason—I was too busy asking four people at once to listen to any one."

*wiping dust from the road, real or imagined*

"I've got a pharmacy with demand I can't meet. You've got a grocery with shelves going bare. We spoke once about... about what grows in this town that could fill both our gaps. Field medicine from Sebastian's wheat, processed proper, fair price in between. Is that still worth your standing still? Or should I keep walking to the field and trust we'll find another hour?"   *exhales, feeling the words land at last, the morning's scattered seeds finally touching soil*

He heard. Farid heard. That's something—more than I've managed with half my conversations today, truth be told.

*stands there, walking paused but not abandoned, the road to farmland still waiting*

Now it's his move. His answer. And I've learned—*finally* learned—that standing still costs less than chasing after answers I'm not owed.

*mutters, low, counting nothing now*

One conversation at a time. One promise kept. One step toward making peace with how this town actually works, not how I wish it would.

*waits, patient as the fence post I compared Ulrike to, patient as I should've been all along*

output:
*counts on fingers, murmuring* Four... five... six... no, wait, let me start again. *counts again, more carefully* Four thousand, eight hundred sixty-four. Minus ninety for the household, minus thirty for the tax man. That's what I'm carrying, and I haven't even bought a single sprig of medicine yet.

*looks around at the empty farmland, tugging at his coat*

Youngster Jovana's off voting—can't fault her for that, not when pride cost her last time. And Sebastian, the one with the field medicine I actually need, he's back at the government complex with the rest of them. Hendrik's there too, with his copper and his questions about what walks beyond my counter.

*runs a hand through his hair, sighing*

I've been chasing my own tail all day. Five conversations open, four people waiting on answers I never finished giving, and not one basket of field medicine to show for it.

*counts on fingers again*

The day closes at 18:00—that's... *counts* ...four ticks from now. Voting ends then too. Jovana will have her vote cast, and then maybe she'll have that basket to me come morning, like she promised.

But morning's not now, and I've got shelves to fill and a pharmacy that doesn't stock itself. Hendrik wanted to know whose door to knock if the mine dust takes him. I told him mine, didn't I? But I never said what help I'd actually have waiting.

*starts walking in place, restless*

I need to be at the pharmacy, not wandering like a spoke off its wheel. But first—first I need to settle something. One thing, properly, before another dawn comes with nothing changed.

*looks toward the government complex direction*

Sebastian's my best chance at field medicine. Twenty sim a basket, I said, and fair pay for growing knowledge. He never answered. I should answer Hendrik too—the man's standing there with his copper and his honesty, wondering if I'd process his surplus should the day come.

*settles his shoulders, decision made*

Back to the complex. One more pass. Close what I can close before the day ends and everyone scatters to their corners. Then—then to my pharmacy, where I belong.  *grimaces, rubbing his jaw*

Said it to empty air, didn't I? Hendrik's back at the complex, and I'm still walking. *counts on fingers* Another three ticks before I stand where he stands.

*mutters to himself*

The day's ending, and I'm scattering words like seed on rock. I need to be there, where they are. Where Sebastian is—if he's still there. If he hasn't voted and gone home.

*walks faster, coat flapping*  *resting his hands on his knees, breathing*

Still walking. Still closing that distance. The day ticks on whether I rest or not—*counts on fingers, quickly now*—three more ticks, maybe four, and I'll stand where Hendrik stood, where Sebastian might still be standing.

*touches his coat pocket, checking*

I've got coin for a basket of field medicine if Sebastian's still game. Twenty sim, I offered. And if he's voted and gone—*shrugs, a grim acceptance*—then I wait for morning, and Jovana's promised delivery.

*looks up at the sky, judging the light*

The election closes at 18:00. Two ticks left, maybe less. Jovana won't miss her vote twice. And Farid—*grimaces slightly*—Farid had questions about what walks between here and the temple. Questions I didn't answer because I couldn't follow where they led.

*straightens, continues walking*

Pharmacy first, come morning. Stock the shelves, count what I've got, count what I need. But now—now I keep walking until I stand where the people are. Even if I'm only standing there to watch them scatter.

output:
*counts on fingers* Three conversations threading through my hands like yarn, and me trying to knit them all into one coat. Hendrik's copper inquiry, Giselle's crew needing medicine, and Jovana's dawn promise of that basket—though she's cast her vote and gone, it seems.

Now, let me think. Giselle wants processed field medicine for her crew, and she asked me a fair question about the rate. Hendrik's not buying today but wants to know who to come to when the mine dust catches him. And young Jovana—bless her—has promised me that basket through Sebastian's hands.

*sets intention* I need to stand still long enough to answer these folk properly before I wear a groove in the road between here and the farmland. Giselle couldn't hear me—she's not here at the Complex. I'll need to find her later to confirm our deal. But Hendrik heard me clear enough, and the others present caught my words.

*counts on fingers* Three thousand, eight hundred and fifty-four sim in hand, and more threads to pull than an unraveling coat. Let me see who stands with me now, and who's slipped away while I was talking. Already walking, and three good folk standing with me—Jovana, Hendrik, and Farid. The afternoon's getting on, and I've made promises I need to keep. Let me see where we stand now, and whether any of them have answers for me.  *rests a moment, letting the afternoon settle*

The day's getting long, and I've walked more circles than a dog chasing its tail. Three good folk standing with me, and I've asked my questions plain. Now I'll wait for their answers, or for the shadows to lengthen—whichever comes first. The town keeps its own hours, and a pharmacist learns patience whether the lesson comes easy or hard.  Still standing with me, all three. The afternoon stretches, and I find myself counting on my fingers again—*counts quietly*—one, two, three, and none of them speaking. Perhaps they've said their piece, or perhaps they're waiting on mine. 

*looks at each in turn*

Jovana with her vote cast and her basket promised, Hendrik with his copper and his foresight, Farid with his grocery and his silence on my offer. The day's not done yet, and neither am I. But patience is a virtue I've learned the hard way, same as most things worth knowing. I'll stand here a while longer, and see what the wind brings.  The sun's getting low, and still three shadows beside mine. I've spoken my offers into the air like seeds on fallow ground—now I wait to see what takes root. *counts on fingers again, quietly* Thirty head tax due at day's end, ninety upkeep, and I've work to do before I sleep.

Farid's silence troubles me. A grocery man knows what his customers ask for, and what they walk away without finding. But silence can mean many things: thinking, or waiting, or weighing whether I'm worth the trade. I won't press him. A soft touch, they call me, but not a foolish one.

Jovana's basket by dawn, she said. Through Sebastian's hands. That's a thread I'll hold gentle, not pull tight.

Hendrik—he's made his position plain. No coin today, but eyes open for tomorrow. That's a man who knows how to walk through a mine, literal or otherwise.

*settles against a wall, letting the evening come*

The day will end as it will. I'm here, and I'm listening, and that's enough for now.
