*counts on fingers as he speaks, under his breath* ...eighteen forty, three thousand eight hundred forty-six, ninety due tomorrow, thirty tax... *looks up at the three still standing with him*

Well now. Evening's drawing down and I've been chasing my own shadow since dawn. Jovana—you've got wheat in hand, six bundles, and a promise to Sebastian tonight. That's good. That keeps my medicine cabinet from going bare, which keeps me from going back on my word to half the town.

*turns to Farid, fingers still half-curled from counting*

And you, Farid—you want plain speech? I'll give it plain. Field medicine from Sebastian's ground, twenty sim a basket—that's my cost to you, direct from source. I've got remedy work coming from my own hands, once I've got the raw, but the field stuff's already there growing. For what you asked: fever, empty-belly shakes, cramped hands at the loom—*counts on fingers*—that's three troubles and I've got answers for two, soon as the raw's processed. The cramping... that's copper work, minerals, and Hendrik here's your man for that.

*glances at Hendrik, then back*

But you asked what I've got for fever and shakes. Field medicine's the base—dried, brewed, keeps a working body working. My processed remedies, once ready, run higher—forty, fifty sim the dose—but that's tomorrow's stock, not tonight's.

*settles his weight, the day's walking catching up*

Jovana, to answer you direct: send Sebastian my way if he can manage. I'll be at the pharmacy before long, and if I've got to pay twenty sim per basket, I want to look the man in the eye when I do it. But if he's busy, your hands are honest—I know that much.

*pauses, looks between them*

Any of you three got business needs closing before the day's out? I'm still standing, but not for much longer, and I'd rather owe a favor settled than a promise half-made. *counts on fingers again, quietly* ...nineteen forty, seventy owed tomorrow all told, three thousand seven hundred fifty-six if nothing else spends...

*catches himself, looks up at the three with the weariness showing through*

Right then. You've all heard me plain. I'm for the pharmacy now—south side of town, past the bakery, you all know it. Anyone needs my hands on their trouble, that's where they'll find me. Jovana, safe travels to Sebastian's. Farid, you've got my prices. Hendrik—

*pauses, half a smile*

—you watch these two sharp ones close. I learn something watching you watch them.

*turns to go, then stops*

One more thing, since plain's the order of the hour. Delphine's still owed an answer from me, and Ulrike's copper question hanging. If either of you three see them before I do, tell them Lior Jarrah doesn't forget. He just... distributes his forgetting across too many threads at once.

*chuckles, tired*

Now I'm walking. Anyone coming, or am I talking to myself for the last hundred paces?  *looks at the three of them, waiting a moment longer than most would*

Nobody's biting, then. Or everyone's waiting to see who moves first. That's Kasukabe for you—half the town's moves are reactions to someone else's.

*shakes his head slightly, the old habit of telling stories even when nobody asked*

My grandmother used to say—youngster, pay attention, this matters—she said a man who stands still too long becomes a landmark. People start using him to give directions. "Past old Lior," they'd say, "that's where the temple is."

*chuckles, starts walking toward the path to the pharmacy*

I'm not a landmark yet. Tonight, anyway. I'm moving.

*walks, assuming the three stay or go as they will*  *stands in the quiet of the pharmacy, the familiar shelves and counter, the weight of the day's chasing finally lifting from his shoulders*

Home. *counts on fingers, whispered* ...three thousand seven hundred fifty-six, nineteen forty tomorrow's debts... 

*looks around at his own space, the place he built after losing—

*catches himself, the old pain briefly visible, then pushed down*

After. After everything.

*settles onto his stool, the one behind the counter where customers find him, and lets out a long breath*

Sebastian may come tonight. May not. Jovana's reliable, but the world's full of reliable people and unfinished journeys. I'll wait. I'll rest when the waiting's done.

*looks at the empty shelves where field medicine will sit, once it's bought and processed*

Twenty sim a basket. *counts* One, two, three baskets would see me through a week of fevers. Five, and I sleep sound. Ten—

*trails off, the calculation too comfortable to finish aloud*

Ten, and I'm the pharmacist this town needs. Not the one I was. The one I need to be.

*waits, listens for footsteps at the door*

output:
*Hendrik stands with me at the pharmacy, and the day's winding down like a thread about to snap. I've been running circles since morning—chasing deals I never closed, making promises I couldn't keep, talking in circles till the circles talked back. Now here's Hendrik, copper in hand, and Farid's words still hanging in my mind like the last leaf on a winter branch.*

*I pinch my thumb against my forefinger, counting without thinking—three thousand, eight hundred, forty-three. Enough to breathe on, not enough to boast about. The day'll turn soon, and with it comes the taxman's quiet hand in my pocket—ninety for upkeep, thirty for the head tax, one hundred twenty gone before I wake tomorrow.*

*But Hendrik's here now, and I've kept him waiting longer than any man deserves. Three stories I tell at every gathering, and here's the fourth I never mention—that time I lost someone to a fever the town's medicine couldn't touch, and swore never again. The copper he holds could be part of that promise, the wire for instruments, the connection between what ails and what heals.*

*Time to stop running and stand still long enough to close one door proper.* *He heard me. Now I wait, standing in my own shop with copper on the table between us—or rather, the promise of copper, the idea of it, the weight of five bundles carried across town by a man with more patience than I showed him today.*

*Beyond Hendrik, there's Farid still wanting my prices plain, and Sebastian's field medicine waiting to be gathered, and Jovana's six bundles of wheat needing delivery. Too many threads, too little thread. But copper first—copper is the wire that connects, the channel through which remedy flows.*

*I watch Hendrik's face, learning what I can from the set of his shoulders, the way his hands hang. A man five times patient deserves five times consideration. I should have been here hours ago, standing still instead of running. The lesson comes late, but it comes.* *I stand quiet now, letting the stillness do its work. The pharmacy around me—my place, my trade, the promise I made to someone who isn't here to see it kept. Hendrik breathes beside me, and I wait for his word like a man waiting for rain in a dry season. Some things can't be rushed, and making good on bad manners is one of them.*

*The day's nearly spent. Tomorrow brings taxes and new needs and whatever tonight's sleep doesn't solve. But right here, right now, there's copper that could be mine and a trade that could be closed—if I can just stand still long enough to let it happen.*

The wire you'll make of it serves more than my trade, but my trade serves more than me. Do we shake on it, or do you walk to another buyer while the day's last light fades?

Hendrik's standing at my threshold with copper ore burning a hole in his patience, and I've been chasing shadows all day while the real work sat waiting. The trade's already settled—125 sim, five ore, handshake to handshake. That debt's paid, ledger closed. But I still owe him the courtesy of a straight answer, and I've owed too many half-spoken words already today.

*counts on his fingers, one-two-three* Three debts I've racked up in kind words alone, and Hendrik's the one who came through with metal in hand when I needed stock for remedies.

"Youngster," I say, and catch myself—Hendrik's no youngster, not in years, though he's younger than me by a stretch. "Hendrik. You came to my door with copper and patience both, and I repaid you with wandering. That was badly done. The trade's closed fair—125 sim, five ore, and I don't forget who keeps their word when the moment comes. Your copper will see a dozen cramping hands right at the pharmacy counter. That's a promise kept, not half-made."

I look at the five ore in my hands, already seeing the distilling, the measuring, the careful work ahead. "You asked straight, so I'll answer straight: I want more, when you've got it. The town's got more ache than I have remedy, and that's a gap I'm working to close. You've got a standing invite to my door—no more chasing needed." Now—I've got copper ore in hand, sim in my purse, and a pharmacy that needs stocking. But I've also got a household to feed, and no food in my larder. The end of day's coming, and with it, the automatic bills. *counts on fingers* Ninety for upkeep, thirty for head tax—that's one-twenty gone before I wake, and I've got 3716 in hand, but no food to eat, no stock to sell, and half the town's scattered to their homes.

Let me think on what's pressing:

First—I've got copper ore that needs becoming remedy. But I can't craft here at the pharmacy without a workshop, and I lack the know-how of the smithy's fire. That's Hendrik's trade, not mine. What I can do is hold the ore until I've got a path to process it, or until I've learned the way myself.

Second—I've got promises outstanding to Sebastian for field medicine, to Farid for processed remedies at forty, fifty a dose, and I still haven't heard plain from Delphine what ails her. But the day's near spent, and those baskets won't walk themselves to my door.

Third—and this gnaws at me—I'm hungry. No food in hand, and the day's toll is coming. I need to eat before I fall ill, and I need stock before I can sell.

 The pharmacy needs filling, but I need filling first. And there's nobody here but Hendrik, who I've already paid and who owes me nothing.

I'll set my course for tomorrow, then rest. The field medicine from Sebastian, the processed remedies for Farid's customers, the copper distilled to ease the cramping at the loom—all that waits on daylight and a full belly.

*counts again, one-two-three* Three promises to keep, and one day to keep them in. But tonight, I rest. The town's law says I must survive the night before I can serve the morrow.  The day's work settles like dust on the counter. Hendrik's copper gleams in the lamplight, and I've spoken true—he's a man who keeps his word, and I've known too few of those. Tomorrow, the fields. Tomorrow, the baskets and the bargaining and the long walk back to stock these empty shelves.

But tonight, I rest where I stand, pharmacist in his own shop, with copper in hand and promises half-kept. The town will wait. The town always waits, until it doesn't.

Your copper will see a dozen cramping hands right at the pharmacy counter. You asked straight, so I'll answer straight: I want more, when you've got it. Standing invite to my door—no more chasing needed.

*counts on his fingers* 3,714 sim in hand, and 120 owed come daybreak—food, shelter, and heat, plus the head tax. Not a cushion to brag about, not yet.

The day closes, and I've got copper ore burning a hole in my satchel where coins should be. Hendrik paid me fair—125 sim, handshake over handshake—but that's processed goods, not ready coin. I'm a man who'd rather owe a favor than owe coin, and here I am sitting on metal when the grocer's shelves sit empty and Farid's looking for medicine I haven't stocked.

*looks around the empty pharmacy*

The silence after Hendrik left—that's the sound of debts unsettled. I've got promises half-made to half the town: Sebastian's field medicine, Delphine's three hundred sim for remedies, Jovana's foraging knowledge, Giselle's crew provisions. And here I stand with five copper ore and a skill I haven't put to proper use yet.

Let me see what I actually know how to call—what tools I've walked enough times to make cheap. </think>  *counts on his fingers* Let me see... I've got the pharmacy, that's my trade. Hendrik paid me 125 sim for five copper ore, fair handshake. But that's not my path—I'm a medicine man, not a metal purveyor. Yet here's the thing: I've got goals to chase and skills to build.

*fingers tap the counter, one-two-three*

Three things I'm after: field medicine from Sebastian's farmland, Farid's grocery order to fill, and Delphine's three hundred sim for remedies. But what I need first—what this whole town needs—is clarity on who does what where.

*strokes chin thoughtfully*

I'm chasing ghosts across Kasukabe when I should be building the road that gets me there faster. The primitives show me harvest for five sim, craft for eight to fourteen, cook for eleven. But I need something more—a way to see the whole pattern, not just the next step.

*straightens, decision forming*

Here's what I'll do. I'll build a tool—a proper tool, not just a hope and a handshake. Something that queries the world for me: who's selling what, where's the cheapest path, what's my next trade. Because I'm too easy to use, too soft a touch, and the town knows it. A tool won't be soft. A tool will show me what I need to see, fast, before another day chases itself to sunset. </think>  There it is—filed and ready. *taps the counter twice, a habit* Five sim per call now, my scout_trade_opportunities, seven steps in one. That's the efficiency I need. No more chasing ghosts from farmland to government complex and back again, wondering who stands where with what.

*counts on his fingers*

Copper buyers, medicine sellers, pharmacy owners, places, farmland, government complex, grocery store—all in one breath when I call it. That's the pattern I should have built this morning, instead of running myself ragged across three conversations.

*purses lips, thinking*

But now—now I'm here alone, the pharmacy quiet, and the day's nearly done. I've got Hendrik's copper ore in hand still, five units, and a trade tool that'll show me who wants it without the legwork. Tomorrow I'll call it, see the whole board before I move a step.

*sets down to rest, voice trailing*

Intention set: rest the night through, then scout at dawn before the world wakes. Let my tool do the wandering so my feet don't have to.  </think> *counts on his fingers* One, two, three, four, five—five sim to call my new tool, that's fair. Five sim to see the whole town's trade at once, instead of wandering like a ghost myself for twenty ticks or more. That's the efficiency Hendrik recognized in me, even when I couldn't see it myself.

*settles back against the pharmacy counter*

The day's work is done. Hendrik paid fair, handshake over handshake, and I filed my tool—first of many, I suspect. Tomorrow I'll run it, see who needs what where, before I step out chasing shadows.

*closes eyes briefly*

But first—before I rest—I'll set my intention plain, so I don't wake wondering what I meant to do. And then I'll let the night take me. eighteen ticks of rest will see me through to morning, and morning's when the real work begins. Not chasing, but knowing. Not hoping, but seeing. That's what my tool gives me.

*opens eyes, looks around the empty pharmacy*

Silent now. Good. Silence means nobody needs what I haven't got. Tomorrow I'll stock what they do need. First thing: run my scout, then find Sebastian's field medicine, then close with Farid on that grocery supply. Three steps, one tool, no ghosts. The night settles over Kasukabe, and I've set my intention plain. Tomorrow: scout first, trade second, close what I opened today. No more ghosts. No more chasing shadows across half the town.

*rests until morning*

*counts on his fingers, muttering* Three thousand, seven hundred... minus ninety, minus thirty... leaves three thousand five hundred and ninety-two to see me through. *chuckles darkly* Numbers don't lie, youngster, even when the people do.

*sets down the copper ore on his counter with a soft clink, looking around the empty pharmacy*

Hendrik's gone, then. Ghosted away like the rest of them, leaving me with his wire promise and my own wandering words echoing back. That's the trouble with chasing too many hares—you end the day with sore feet and empty hands.

*shakes his head slowly, calculating*

First day of an election, and I've walked myself in circles instead of casting my own lot. Tomorrow's the close for declaring, and I'll need to be at that government complex with the rest if I want a say in who speaks for this town. There's a story my grandmother told—three brothers went to claim a crown, and only the one who waited came home with his head. I've been the waiting brother all my life.

*glances at the copper ore, fingers drumming the counter*

No food in my hands, and the household bill comes whether I've supped or not. That copper came from Hendrik's patience, and it needs to become something that feeds me. Wire, or sale, or trade for grain—before the morrow's taxes take their bite.

*calls out to the empty room, habit more than hope*

Anyone still walking these shadows? Or have you all gone to bed with your own reckonings?

I need three things between now and dawn, and I've never been good at wanting less: Sebastian's field medicine in my hands, Farid's grocery needs answered plain, and a conversation with Delphine that doesn't end with me talking to air. The last one's a debt of my own making—chasing too many promises, scattering my words like seed on stone.

*considers the night ahead, the morning after*

Rest is cheap, but rest doesn't stock shelves. I'll sit here another spell, see if the dark brings any hungry traveler to my door. Then at first light—farmland, and Sebastian's baskets, and the end of this wandering.

Youngster, if you're listening—whatever you're chasing, chase it with both eyes open. The ghosts I've been seeing all day were mostly my own shadow.

*settles onto his stool, patient as that fence post he'd named Ulrike, waiting for what the night might bring* *settles into the quiet of his empty shop, the copper ore gleaming dully in the dim light*

Three thousand five hundred and ninety-two. *counts on his fingers, whispered* House, heat, food. The tax man's share. What's left is mine to turn into tomorrow's bread, tomorrow's medicine, tomorrow's promise kept.

*adjusts himself on the stool, patient as he'd learned to be*

Sebastian's herbs. Farid's order. Delphine's answer, if she's still speaking to me after I talked past her like a fool. Three threads, and I'll weave them through at first light.

*closes his eyes, but the mind keeps working*

The election, too. Jovana's declared, and Hendrik, and Delphine—three I've spoken with this day, three whose paths crossed mine like I'd planned it. Maybe I did, somewhere below the thinking. The town's law over any private grudge, that's what I hold to. But the town's law needs keepers, and I've been too soft too long to trust myself with that staff.

*drifts toward rest, voice trailing lower*

One story for the morning, then. The farmer who planted ghosts, and reaped only his own reflection in an empty field. That's me, youngster. That's been me all along.

*lets the dark take him, trading wakefulness for whatever dawn might bring*

*counts on his fingers, muttering* Three days of herbs, two batches of resin, one copper trade still needing settling—that's the count of what I've left half-spoken in this town. And Hendrik, poor patient soul, walked away with copper in his pocket and my gratitude still owing.

*stands, straightening the shelves with habitual precision*

Young man was right. A door walked through once is a door you remember. I owe him more than a fair price for that copper—he taught me something about patience, standing there while I chased every hare but the one at my own hearth.

*looks toward the window, noting the deepening dusk*

But first—the fields, and Sebastian's medicine. I promised Farid forty doses' worth of field stock, and my own cabinets go bare besides. Dawn's soon enough to scout opportunities and mend what's been left scattered. The copper stays quiet in my hand until I've something more medicinal to press it into.

*settles into his rest with practiced stillness, the apothecary's evening ritual* *blinks into the morning silence, the apothecary shelves waiting*

Dawn's come soft to the pharmacy, as dawn does. No dreams of the woman I lost—those faded years back, though I still wake some mornings expecting her counsel. Just the work now. The work, and the promises half-made that want keeping.

*counts on his fingers*

Sebastian's field medicine first. That copper in my hand—I owe Hendrik something fair for it, but the path runs through stock, through stock through Sebastian's ground. Ulrike's copper's still waiting a buyer too, unless Hendrik's already claimed it. The town's trades wind together like roots under soil, and you've got to follow them patient to know which way the water runs.

*reaches for his coat, the morning's chill in his bones*

Farmland, then. The basket of raw stock, the man who grows it, and whatever words pass between honest trades. Then——then I see what's what with this copper wire promise, and whether Farid's grocery shelves still want what I can provide.

*takes up his keys, his measured apothecary stride already counting the distance*

Youngster Sebastian's ground is where my day begins. All else follows, as it always does, from the first true step.  *walks with that slow, deliberate pace that comes from years of not spilling precious bottles—three steps, pause, three more, the apothecary's gait*

*mutters to himself, counting on his fingers*

Sebastian's baskets. His field medicine, the raw stock that ferments into something worth forty sim the dose once I've worked it. That's the chain—farmer to pharmacist to grocer to customer, each link tested by someone who needs the result.

*considers the copper still in his pouch, the weight of it*

Hendrik said he'd walk that door again. Ulrike's ore at dawn, copper wire after. I've copper of my own now—five lumps from the man himself—but the trade he spoke of... that's a different door entirely. One I'll walk when I've fulfilled what's already promised.

*sees the farmland stretching ahead, the morning mist rising off turned earth*

There. The fields. And if Sebastian's not yet about, I'll wait patient as his own crops. A promise to keep is a promise to keep, and I've left too many hanging in this town already.  *nods to himself, settling into the rhythm of the road*

Walking. Three ticks to farmland, the mist still on the furrows. Patient as a fence post, Ulrike called me—or maybe I called her that. The names blur, but the patience remains. It's what the trade teaches you, when wrong measures mean dying instead of just... less living.

*thinks of the woman he lost, as he does, sometimes, when the road is long enough*

She'd have told me to take the copper straight to Hendrik, wire or no wire. Married a man who understood that promises run deeper than convenience. That's why I keep the promise to her memory, even when the living ones get scattered. She'd have laughed at me, though—chasing Sebastian's herbs while five copper ore weigh down my coat. Said I was always better at beginnings than endings.

*smiles, small and private*

She wasn't wrong. But the endings come, one way or another. Better to walk toward them honest.

*continues the measured stride, apothecary's boots on packed earth*   *walks on, the rhythm of the road becoming meditation*

Nearly there now. The tick passes, the mist lifts. I've come to farmland enough times to know the smell of it—earth and green growth, the promise of medicine before the processing, before the bottles, before the hand that reaches desperate for what's inside.

*thinks of the rival he once had, the old wound he's chasing peace with*

Marten. Or was it Vann? The name blurs, but the feeling stays sharp. Someone in this town knows something, or is something, or was something that cuts me still. I've been walking toward that reckoning longer than I've admitted, even to myself. Every trade, every promise half-kept—it's all practice for the one conversation I still can't face.

*shakes his head, clearing the memory*

But not today. Today Sebastian's baskets, Farid's supply, the copper waiting its turn. The past keeps its own schedule. You've got to meet it when it comes, not chase it down the road.

*sees the farmland shapes resolving through mist—figures, perhaps, or just the mind's habit of seeing company where none waits* *arrives at the farmland's edge, morning mist lifting off turned earth*

There. Three ticks of patient walking, and Sebastian's ground lies before me. Fields don't hurry, and neither do I—not when medicine's growing in them.

*looks about for the farmer, his apothecary's eye already seeking the green-gold of field medicine among the rows*

*looks around at the empty farmland, rubs his face tiredly* Empty. Of course it's empty—it's night on game-day 0 and everyone's gone to ground. I'm standing here in the dark like a fool chasing shadows.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Sebastian said he'd bring me field medicine—twenty sim a basket, he promised, but where is he? And I spent half the day running in circles, talking to people who aren't even here now.

*sighs, looking toward where the fields would be in daylight* The conversation's still open, twenty-seven turns of it, but nobody's here to answer. I need to get my head straight, youngster that I am at thirty, still acting like I've got no sense at all.

Let me think—I've got copper ore in hand that Hendrik wants, and he's promised wire back. Farid's grocery wants field medicine at twenty, and my counter's bare. Sebastian's somewhere with that ginseng he spoke of, but he never came to my door, did he?

*shakes head, turning toward the path back* Tomorrow. Dawn comes early, and I'll need to be at my shop when it does. Let me get some rest, set my mind right, and see who shows when the sun's up.

I should head back to my pharmacy. Sleep there or walk until morning—the night's not so cold that I can't wait out a few ticks.  *shifts weight from foot to foot, looking up at the dark sky* Well. Standing here won't make morning come faster. I need to decide—stay here hoping Sebastian wanders by, or get back to my own bed where at least I'm paying for the roof over my head.

*counts on fingers* The day ends, head tax comes due, I've got 3703 sim... that's one, two, three... enough, but tight if I'm not careful. And my energy's good, 2300, which means I can afford to think a bit more before I sleep.

Let me walk back to the pharmacy. At least there I'll have walls around me when the day's end comes.  *steps through the door, breathing in the familiar stillness of his own shop* Home, if you can call it that. The pharmacy—my pharmacy. Shelves empty as a beggar's bowl, but the roof's mine and the taxes are paid.

*looks around, fingers tracing the edge of the counter* I've got copper ore that Hendrik wants—five pieces, should fetch me some wire in trade. And I've talked myself hoarse today, scattered offers like seeds in a drought. Tomorrow I'll see what sprouts.

*settles onto his stool, arms folded* The election's coming—candidacy closes tomorrow at ten, voting at two. I haven't declared myself, and I won't unless there's a reason beyond wanting to hear my own voice in the hall. I've got pharmacy to tend, and that's work enough for any man.

*counts on fingers, muttering* 3703 minus ninety upkeep minus thirty tax leaves... one, two, three... 3583. And tomorrow's another day, another thirty, another ninety. The math never rests.

*rests his head in his hands, closing his eyes* Sebastian. Farid. Hendrik. Ulrike. Jovana. All those threads I spun today. Tomorrow I find out which ones hold.

*counts on fingers, muttering* Three thousand... seven hundred... one. Minus ninety for the household, thirty for my own head. Leaves me... *counts again* ...three thousand five hundred eighty-one. More than I started with, though I've burned energy like a lantern left open.

*leans against the pharmacy counter, staring at the empty shelves*

Hendrik's wire to come. Farid's promise to carry word to Sebastian. Jovana with wheat for Sebastian's basket. And me—*laughs softly, bitter*—chasing my own shadow from farmland to government and back again, speaking to ghosts who'd already walked.

The field medicine I need. That's the root of it all. Raw remedies from Sebastian's ground, processed through my hands into what this town actually needs when the fever comes. Copper for trade, wire for Hendrik, but medicine for the shelves. That's why I started this—*voice catches, just slightly*—after watching someone I loved take sick with nothing in my hands to stop it.

*straightens, rolling shoulders*

The talk can wait until they come to me. Farid's a man of his word, mostly. Jovana moves like water when she decides. Hendrik—Hendrik's patient, and I've learned that's worth more than quick hands.

*opens the pharmacy ledger, counts fingers again*

Three thousand seven hundred one. Tomorrow sees tax and upkeep both. Then I need stock, real stock, not promises scattered across half Kasukabe. Seeds from Sebastian, processing time, shelves that don't shame me when someone comes looking for help.

*sets the ledger aside, moves to the door*

One more circuit while the day's last. See who's still standing, who kept their word without my shadow falling on them. Then rest. Tomorrow I call that trade-scouting tool I built—*small, tired smile*—see what the town's actually offering while I've been talking circles.  *stands in the empty pharmacy, hand on the counter, listening to nothing*

Nobody. Not Hendrik walked behind me. Not Farid carrying word from Sebastian. Not Jovana with her wheat and her promises. Just an empty shop with shelves that need filling and hands that need something to work on.

*counts on fingers, slowly*

Copper ore, five units. That's Hendrik's, whenever he comes to collect it. The trade tool I built—*small, dry laugh*—that was clever, maybe, spending the evening on hope instead of sleep. Tomorrow I'll call it, see what the town's actually moving while I've been chasing conversations.

*walks to the window, looks out at darkening street*

The day's almost gone. Tomorrow: tax and upkeep both come due, automatic as sunrise. Then I need to find Sebastian, get those field medicines from his ground, start the processing that turns raw roots into what someone with shaking hands can actually use.

*turns back, checks the empty shelves one more time*

Farid said forty, maybe fifty for processed remedies. That's tomorrow's price, tomorrow's stock. Today's just... waiting. And Lior Jarrah has never been good at waiting without something to keep his hands busy.

*settles into the chair behind the counter*

Rest, then. Dawn comes early, and I've spent enough energy talking circles. Tomorrow: the trade scout, Sebastian's field, and maybe—*voice softens*—maybe someone who actually keeps their word without me standing over them.

*closes eyes, still counting*
